questions.title: Post-fracture DVT complicates to pulmonary thromboembolism
questions.question: 76-year-old woman is hospitalized after falling and fracturing her left femoral trochanter. Two weeks later, the left leg is swollen, particularly below the knee. She experiences pain on movement of the leg; on palpation, there is tenderness. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur after these events?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gangrenous necrosis of the foot would require arterial, not venous, compromise -- unrelated to the swelling and tenderness pattern described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A hematoma of the thigh would be a localized bleeding collection, not the leg swelling and calf tenderness pattern this vignette describes.
explanations.C: Correct. Leg swelling, pain on movement and tenderness two weeks after a hip fracture, with continued immobilization, is the classic picture of deep vein thrombosis in the leg veins. Such a thrombus can detach and travel via venous return to the lung, making pulmonary thromboembolism the most likely subsequent complication. This is the expected downstream risk of an immobilization-related DVT.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic venous congestion is a systemic pattern from right heart failure, not the localized limb finding described, and not the acute complication being asked about.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a systemic, widespread coagulation disorder, not the localized, mechanical leg-swelling process described here.

questions.title: Immobilization causes leg DVT through venous stasis
questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has had discomfort and swelling of the left leg for the past week. On physical examination, the leg is slightly difficult to move, but on palpation, there is no pain. A venogram shows thrombosis of deep left leg veins. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely to cause this condition?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Turbulent flow is more typically implicated in arterial or cardiac thrombus formation (e.g. at vessel bifurcations), not the classic mechanism for a leg deep vein thrombosis like this.
explanations.B: Correct. Immobilization produces venous stasis -- stagnant, slow-moving blood in the leg veins -- one arm of Virchow's triad predisposing to thrombus formation. A leg that has been difficult to move for a week, with confirmed deep vein thrombosis, fits this stasis mechanism most directly. This is the standard mechanism tested for an immobility-associated DVT.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypercalcemia is not a standard, directly-tested risk factor for venous thrombosis in this context.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent that would reduce, not promote, thrombosis risk.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Nitric oxide is a vasodilator and platelet-inhibitor that would tend to reduce, not promote, thrombosis.

questions.title: A detached intravascular mass is called an embolus
questions.question: A detached intravascular mass carried by the blood from its point of origin to a distant site is called:

explanations.A: Correct. An embolus is by definition a detached intravascular mass -- solid, liquid or gaseous -- carried by the bloodstream from its point of origin to lodge at a distant site. This is precisely the definition given in the stem. The term describes the mass once it has detached and is travelling, not before.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An infarct is the area of tissue necrosis that can result once an embolus (or other cause) obstructs blood flow, not the travelling mass itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A thrombus is the mass before it detaches and starts travelling -- once detached and travelling, it is termed an embolus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A clot describes coagulated blood forming after death or outside the vasculature, not a detached, travelling intravascular mass.

questions.title: Neck vein stab wound risks air embolism
questions.question: A patient admits to the emergency unit after a neck vein stabbing wound. What type of emboli would you most suspect to occur in this patient?

explanations.A: Correct. An open, low-pressure venous injury near the heart, such as a stab wound to a neck vein, allows atmospheric air to be drawn into the venous circulation during inspiration. This produces an air embolism, the specific hemodynamic risk of this type of injury. Neck veins are particularly susceptible because of their low venous pressure and proximity to the heart.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tumour emboli arise from malignancy shedding cells into the circulation, unrelated to an acute traumatic neck vein injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thrombotic emboli arise from a pre-existing thrombus, not from an acute open venous wound allowing air entrainment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fat emboli classically arise from a bone fracture releasing marrow fat, not from a neck vein stab wound.

questions.title: Red infarction is seen in the lung
questions.question: A red infarction is seen in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The heart has a single (coronary) blood supply and shows a pale infarct, not a red one.
explanations.B: Correct. A red (hemorrhagic) infarct occurs when blood re-enters the necrotic area, typically in an organ with a dual or collateral blood supply. The lung, supplied by both pulmonary and bronchial arteries, is the standard example. This dual supply lets blood re-enter the infarcted zone, giving it its characteristic red, hemorrhagic appearance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The brain, though it has some collateral circulation via the circle of Willis, is not the standard example given for a red infarct in this pairing -- it is instead the standard exception for liquefactive necrosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The kidney has a single, end-arterial blood supply and shows a pale infarct, not a red one.

questions.title: Cerebral infarction is liquefactive necrosis
questions.question: Cerebral infarction is:

explanations.A: Correct. Cerebral infarction undergoes liquefactive necrosis, unlike infarction in most other organs. The brain's high lipid content and lack of firm connective-tissue stroma mean the dead tissue is digested into a soft, liquefied cavity rather than retaining firm architecture. This is a specifically-tested exception to the general solid-organ coagulative-necrosis pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Caseation necrosis is the cheese-like necrosis characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections, not the pattern seen in a cerebral infarct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in immune-mediated vascular injury (e.g. malignant hypertension, vasculitis), not the typical pattern of a cerebral infarct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coagulative necrosis is the pattern seen in most other solid-organ infarcts (kidney, spleen, heart), but the brain is the standard exception, undergoing liquefactive necrosis instead.

questions.title: Fat embolism originates from bone fracture
questions.question: Fat embolism can originate from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pregnancy is the classic origin of amniotic fluid embolism, not fat embolism.
explanations.B: Correct. Fat embolism arises when marrow fat is released into the venous circulation, most commonly from a long-bone fracture, where disrupted marrow fat globules enter torn venules at the fracture site. This is the standard clinical origin of fat embolism among the options here. It is a well-recognised complication of long-bone trauma or orthopaedic surgery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Congestive heart failure causes chronic passive congestion, not the origin of a fat embolus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Detached thrombi cause ordinary thromboembolism, a distinct embolus type from fat embolism.

questions.title: Infarction needs acute ischaemia with poor collaterals
questions.question: Infarction is due to:

options.B: acute ischaemia in presence of good collateral circulation
options.C: acute ischaemia in presence of poor collateral circulation

explanations.A: Incorrect. Putrefaction is postmortem microbial decomposition, unrelated to the vascular mechanism of infarction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Good collateral circulation can maintain enough perfusion to prevent necrosis despite the primary vessel's occlusion, so it typically prevents, rather than causes, infarction.
explanations.C: Correct. Infarction results from acute ischaemia occurring specifically in the presence of poor collateral circulation. Without adequate collateral supply, sudden occlusion of the primary vessel cuts off perfusion completely, and the tissue undergoes necrosis. This combination -- acute onset plus poor collaterals -- is what distinguishes infarction from ischaemia that the tissue can tolerate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gradual ischaemia allows time for collateral vessels to develop, making infarction less likely than with acute onset.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Toxemia is a systemic condition, not the direct vascular mechanism of infarction.

questions.title: Solid organ infarcts from arterial occlusion are pale
questions.question: Infarcts occurs due to of arterial occlusion in solid organs such as the kidneys and heart are:

explanations.A: Correct. A pale (anaemic) infarct occurs in a solid organ with a single, end-arterial blood supply -- the kidney and heart are the standard examples. Arterial occlusion cuts off blood entirely, with no second source re-entering the necrotic zone. This lack of re-perfusion is why these infarcts appear pale rather than red.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Caseous describes a necrosis texture (as in tuberculosis), not the standard colour term for an infarct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Black is not the standard colour term used for this type of infarct; that describes a different process such as dry gangrene.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Red infarcts occur in dual-blood-supply organs (such as the lung), not in single-supply solid organs like the kidney and heart.

questions.title: Ischaemia results from arterial obstruction
questions.question: Ischaemia can result from:

explanations.A: Correct. Ischaemia -- inadequate blood supply to a tissue -- most directly results from arterial obstruction, which cuts off the arterial inflow a tissue depends on. This is the direct, standard mechanism tested for producing ischaemia. Removing the tissue's arterial supply at its source is the most immediate route to inadequate perfusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capillary damage can compromise local exchange but is not the standard, direct mechanism of ischaemia tested here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chronic venous congestion primarily impairs venous drainage, a different mechanism from inadequate arterial inflow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Venous obstruction impairs outflow (causing congestion), not the arterial inflow that defines ischaemia.

questions.title: Pale pyramidal renal lesion is coagulative necrosis
questions.question: Microscopic examination of tissue taken from pyramidal shape pale lesion of the kidney showed that the outline of the cells still present but cellular details are lost. Which of the following pathologic conditions most likely present?

explanations.A: Correct. Infarcts in solid organs such as the kidney undergo coagulative necrosis, in which cells die but their basic outline and tissue architecture are preserved for some days, while cellular detail is lost. This is the classic pathological picture of a pyramidal, pale, wedge-shaped renal infarct. Intracellular proteins denature and resist proteolysis, giving this preserved-outline appearance before eventual clearance by inflammatory cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fatty change is intracellular lipid accumulation, a reversible injury pattern, not the preserved-outline, lost-detail picture of an infarct.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Liquefactive necrosis liquefies the tissue and loses architecture entirely (as in the brain), the opposite of preserved cell outlines.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gangrene describes a clinical/gross pattern (usually of a limb or bowel), not this specific microscopic renal picture.

questions.title: Atherosclerosis is the commonest cause of chronic ischaemia
questions.question: The commonest cause of chronic ischaemia is:

options.A: Surgical ligation of a blood vessel

explanations.A: Incorrect. Surgical ligation is an acute, deliberate cause of vessel occlusion, not the commonest driver of chronic ischaemia at a population level.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Infection is not the commonest cause of chronic ischaemia; it can contribute to vascular injury in specific settings but is far less common overall.
explanations.C: Correct. Atherosclerosis -- progressive narrowing of arteries by lipid-laden plaque -- is the commonest cause of chronic ischaemia. It gradually reduces arterial luminal calibre over years, limiting blood flow to the tissue it supplies. This gradual, cumulative process affects far more patients overall than the acute or uncommon alternatives listed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Spasmodic vascular disease (such as Raynaud phenomenon) is a less common cause of chronic ischaemia compared with atherosclerosis.

questions.title: Detached thrombi are the most frequent embolism type
questions.question: The most frequent type of embolism is produced by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fat embolism, though a well-known named entity from bone fracture, is much less frequent overall than ordinary thromboembolism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Malignant (tumour) cell emboli are an uncommon embolus type compared with thromboembolism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Air emboli arise from specific traumatic or iatrogenic settings and are far less frequent overall than thromboembolism.
explanations.D: Correct. Among the recognised embolus types, detached thrombi (thromboembolism) are the most frequent, since deep vein thrombosis and cardiac mural thrombi are common clinical events that regularly source emboli. This makes thromboembolism far more common overall than fat, tumour or air embolism. It is the mechanism behind the great majority of clinically significant emboli.

questions.title: Post-endocarditis splenic wedge lesion is coagulative necrosis
questions.question: The spleen of a 26 year old male who died from complications of subacute bacterial endocarditis is seen at autopsy. On sectioning reveals a tan to white, wedge-shaped lesion with base on the capsule. This finding most likely represents the result of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. An abscess would show a pus-filled cavity, not a firm, tan-to-white wedge-shaped solid lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Caseous necrosis is the cheese-like necrosis characteristic of tuberculosis, not the finding described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Liquefactive necrosis would produce a soft, liquefied area, not a firm, tan-to-white wedge with preserved architecture.
explanations.D: Correct. A tan-to-white, wedge-shaped lesion with its base on the capsule is the classic gross appearance of a splenic infarct, undergoing coagulative necrosis -- the same solid-organ necrosis pattern seen in the kidney. In subacute bacterial endocarditis, septic emboli from valve vegetations commonly lodge in the spleen, producing this wedge-shaped infarct. Coagulative necrosis preserves the tissue's architectural outline even as the cells die.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Metaplasia is a reversible change of one differentiated cell type to another, not the necrosis pattern of an infarct.

questions.title: Leg veins are a common source of pulmonary embolism
questions.question: which of the following sites of thrombi can be the source pulmonary embolism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. An aortic thrombus, being on the arterial side, would embolise systemically, not to the lung.
explanations.B: Correct. Leg (deep) veins are the classic and most common source of thrombi that embolise to the lung as a pulmonary embolus. A detached leg-vein thrombus travels with venous return through the right heart into the pulmonary arterial circulation. This venous-to-pulmonary pathway is why leg veins, specifically, are the site most implicated in pulmonary embolism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A left ventricular (mural) thrombus is on the arterial/systemic side of the circulation and would embolise systemically, not to the lung.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A leg artery thrombus, being arterial, would embolise systemically (e.g. to the distal limb), not to the lung.
